name: Design a Distributed Transaction Coordinator
intent: Make a change that touches several shards or services happen on all of them or on none, even when the coordinator or a participant crashes in the middle, and keep the locks that protect the change from piling up.
codeTitle: two-phase commit with a coordinator log and recovery
finalIntro: One transaction that moves money across three shards, committed atomically.
prompt: Design a transaction coordinator that other services call to commit one atomic change across several independent databases or shards. It must give all-or-nothing results even if the coordinator, a participant or the network fails at any moment, and it must say what happens to the locks while it recovers.
functional: Begin a transaction and let an application enlist several participants in it
Commit atomically: every participant applies its part, or none does
Roll back on request, on a refusal by any participant, or on a timeout
After a crash of the coordinator or of a participant, finish every transaction that was in progress
Report the outcome of any transaction id to anyone who asks, including a participant that is unsure
Offer a different mode for long-running work that cannot hold locks
nonFunctional: Atomicity is never violated: no transaction ends committed on one participant and aborted on another
A decision that was reported to the client is never lost, even if the coordinator machine is destroyed
A commit adds only two network round trips and a few forced log writes to the latency
Handle tens of thousands of transactions per second by running many coordinators
A failure should block as few transactions and as few locks as possible, and for as short a time as possible
Locks are not held forever: timeouts and deadlock handling bound the damage

firstAttempt.text: The application writes to each shard in turn. It starts a local transaction on shard A, one on shard B and one on shard C, makes its changes, and then commits them one after another. If a commit fails, it tries to undo the earlier ones by hand.
limits: A crash between the first and second commit leaves the change half applied, and nobody knows which half
A failed commit after earlier ones succeeded cannot be undone: the earlier commits are already visible to others
There is no record of what the application intended, so nothing can finish or clean up after a crash
A participant that is slow cannot be told apart from one that is dead, so retries risk applying a change twice
Every application would have to invent its own recovery, and each would get it wrong in a different way

steps.title: Ask everyone to promise, then tell everyone to commit
steps.problem: Committing on each shard separately can be interrupted halfway, and once a shard has committed it cannot take its change back.
steps.fix: Put a coordinator in front. In phase one it sends 'prepare' to every participant. Each participant does the work, takes locks on what it touched, writes a 'prepared' record to its own log and only then answers yes. A participant that answers yes has promised that it can commit and will not unilaterally change its mind. In phase two, if every answer is yes the coordinator tells all to commit, and if any answer is no, or missing, it tells all to abort. Participants apply the decision, release their locks and acknowledge.
steps.tradeoff: Atomicity is possible at last, because no one commits before everyone has promised. The price is two network round trips, a forced log write at each participant, and locks held across both round trips instead of for one local commit.

steps.title: Make the decision durable before telling anyone
steps.problem: If the coordinator crashes after some participants committed and its decision is only in memory, a restarted coordinator would not know what it had decided, and the shards would end up split.
steps.fix: The commit decision is the point of no return, so it is written to the coordinator's log and forced to disk before a single 'commit' message is sent. Before that record exists the transaction is not committed, and afterwards it certainly is. When the coordinator restarts, a recovery job reads the log, finds every transaction with a commit record and no 'end' record, and sends the missing commits again. Participants apply a repeated commit once, because commit and abort are idempotent per transaction id. When all acknowledge, an 'end' record lets the log be trimmed.
steps.tradeoff: Recovery is deterministic: the log alone says what every transaction's outcome is. It costs one forced write on the critical path, which group commit spreads over many transactions, and the log must be kept on disks that survive the machine.

steps.title: Bound the blocking with timeouts and presumed abort
steps.problem: A participant that voted yes cannot decide alone. If the coordinator disappears, it is in doubt and must keep its locks, and everyone who needs those rows waits.
steps.fix: Everything before the yes vote can time out safely. A participant that has not been asked to prepare for too long aborts by itself, and a coordinator that does not get all votes in time decides abort. After the yes vote, a participant keeps its locks and repeatedly asks the coordinator for the outcome. With presumed abort the coordinator only logs commit decisions, and answers 'abort' for any transaction it has no commit record for, so aborts need no forced writes and no records to keep. A participant can also ask its peers: if any of them knows the outcome, or never voted yes, the question is settled.
steps.tradeoff: Most failures resolve quickly and aborts are cheap. The prepared window remains: a participant that voted yes has to wait for the coordinator to come back, and the only safe alternative to waiting is to guess, which breaks atomicity.

steps.title: Keep the lock window short and break deadlocks
steps.problem: Prepared participants hold their locks while the coordinator decides, and two transactions that take the same rows in opposite order on different shards wait for each other forever.
steps.fix: Keep the prepared window small: the application sends all its work first, the coordinator prepares everything in parallel, and read-only participants leave after phase one without a second phase. A transaction with only one participant skips the protocol and commits locally. Lock waits have a time limit, and a deadlock check, either by building a wait-for graph across shards or by wound-wait ordering on transaction age, aborts one victim so the other proceeds. Hot rows are updated last in the transaction to shorten the time they are held.
steps.tradeoff: Most transactions hold locks for a few milliseconds, and no cycle waits forever. Aborts caused by timeouts and deadlock victims must be retried by the application, and a hot row still limits throughput to one over its lock hold time.

steps.title: Replicate the coordinator so a crash does not block
steps.problem: A single coordinator is a single point of blocking: if its machine is gone for ten minutes, every in-doubt participant holds its locks for ten minutes.
steps.fix: Store the decision log in a replicated state machine, using Raft or Paxos on three or five nodes, instead of one local disk. A decision counts once a majority has it. Standby coordinators watch for a missing leader, and the new one reads the replicated log, sends the missing commits and answers participants within seconds. Many independent coordinator groups run at once, with transaction ids assigned so each transaction has exactly one owner group. This is the idea of Paxos Commit and of Spanner, where each participant is itself a replicated group.
steps.tradeoff: The blocking window falls from the repair time of a machine to an election time, and a decision survives the loss of any minority of nodes. Each decision costs a replication round trip, and the cluster needs enough nodes in separate failure domains.

steps.title: Use sagas or timestamps when locks are the wrong tool
steps.problem: Holding locks across a long business process, a third party or a slow network is unacceptable, yet some of the work must still end up all-or-nothing.
steps.fix: For long work, split the process into local transactions, each with a compensating action, and run them as a saga. Atomicity is traded for eventual consistency, and intermediate states are visible. For short database work that needs reads without blocking, use timestamp-based commit as in Percolator and Spanner: writes carry a commit timestamp, readers see a snapshot as of a timestamp without taking locks, and the commit of the whole transaction is decided by atomically flipping one primary record. Spanner adds TrueTime, so commit waits out the clock uncertainty and timestamps order transactions across the planet.
steps.tradeoff: Sagas hold no locks and survive slow steps, but expose partial states and need compensations that can themselves fail. Timestamps give lock-free consistent reads, but need an oracle or tightly bounded clocks and still write-lock the rows being changed.

failures.scenario: The coordinator crashes before it logs a decision
failures.impact: Every participant that voted yes is in doubt and holds its locks, and new transactions on those rows wait.
failures.answer: No commit record exists, so on restart the answer is 'abort' for all of them, and each participant rolls back and releases its locks. With a replicated coordinator the standby gives the same answer within seconds. Nothing can be half committed, because no commit message was ever sent.

failures.scenario: The coordinator crashes after logging commit but before telling every participant
failures.impact: Some participants have committed, others are still prepared, and clients may already have been told yes.
failures.answer: The recovery job finds the commit record without an end record and sends commit to every participant, in a loop until each acknowledges. Participants that have already committed ignore the repeat. A prepared participant that asks its peers meanwhile learns the outcome from the ones that committed.

failures.scenario: A participant crashes after voting yes
failures.impact: The coordinator already decided commit, but that shard has not applied the change, and its memory of the locks is gone.
failures.answer: The participant's prepared record is on its own disk, so on restart it reacquires the locks for every prepared transaction before accepting any new work, and asks the coordinator for the outcome. The coordinator keeps resending its decision until it gets an acknowledgement, so the participant ends with the same outcome as the others.

failures.scenario: A participant is slow and the vote times out
failures.impact: The coordinator cannot tell a slow shard from a dead one, and waiting longer holds locks on every other shard.
failures.answer: Waiting for votes is safe to stop: after the timeout the coordinator decides abort, which needs no log record under presumed abort. If the slow shard votes yes later, it asks, learns 'abort' and rolls back. The timeout is tuned from the latency distribution so that it is rarely hit by healthy shards.

failures.scenario: Two transactions wait for each other on different shards
failures.impact: Transaction 1 holds a row on shard A and wants one on B, transaction 2 holds that row on B and wants the one on A. Neither can finish, and the locks stay held.
failures.answer: A lock wait has a limit, and a deadlock check looks for cycles across shards or applies wound-wait ordering by transaction age. One victim is aborted through the normal abort path, which releases its locks, and the application retries it with a short random delay.

alternatives.title: How to get atomicity across services

options.name: Two-phase commit with a coordinator
options.pro: Real atomicity and isolation, with no visible partial states
options.con: Locks held across round trips, and in-doubt blocking when the coordinator is lost

options.name: Saga with compensations
options.pro: No locks, works across companies and slow steps
options.con: Partial states are visible, and compensations must be written and may fail

options.name: Timestamp-based commit (Percolator, Spanner)
options.pro: Lock-free snapshot reads, and atomic commit by flipping one record
options.con: Needs a timestamp oracle or bounded clocks, and writers still lock

options.name: Avoid the problem: keep the data on one shard
options.pro: A local transaction, the cheapest and simplest
options.con: Not always possible, and the design has to be chosen early

alternatives.pick: Keep related data together first. Use two-phase commit where atomicity and isolation matter within one organisation, and a saga across company or long-running boundaries.

alternatives.title: How to protect against a lost coordinator

options.name: Single coordinator with a local log
options.con: Blocking lasts as long as the repair of the machine

options.name: Replicated coordinator log (Raft or Paxos)
options.pro: Blocking lasts only an election, and decisions survive the loss of a machine
options.con: A replication round trip per decision

options.name: Three-phase commit
options.pro: Non-blocking if the network never partitions
options.con: Wrong under partitions and with asynchronous delays, so it is rarely used

options.name: Participants are themselves replicated groups (Spanner)
options.con: A coordinator is still needed, and the system is complex

alternatives.pick: A replicated coordinator log. Make participants replicated too if their loss would block a hot path.

alternatives.title: What a participant does while it is in doubt

options.name: Wait for the coordinator
options.con: Locks held for as long as the coordinator is away

options.name: Ask the other participants
options.pro: Resolves the case where some shard has already learnt the outcome
options.con: If every shard is still prepared, none can decide

options.name: Decide alone after a timeout (heuristic outcome)
options.con: May contradict the real decision, and a human has to repair the mismatch

alternatives.pick: Wait, but ask peers, and allow a heuristic decision only as a manual operator action.

alternatives.title: Where the coordinator runs

options.name: Inside the application (library)
options.pro: No extra service and no extra hop
options.con: The decision log dies with the application server

options.name: A separate coordinator service with its own log
options.pro: The log outlives any application server and recovery runs on its own
options.con: One more service to operate and keep available

options.name: One of the participants coordinates
options.pro: Fewer parts, and the decision shares a log with a participant's data
options.con: Ties the lifetime of the transaction to that shard

alternatives.pick: A separate coordinator service with a replicated log, run as many independent groups.
